title: Meet the Fockers
full_review:
A good deal of star power has gone into the sequel to "Meet the Parents," but as with another recent release, "Ocean's Twelve," the chief pleasure derives from watching them go through their anything-for-a-laugh paces so gamely.

The glossy "Meet the Fockers" (Universal) picks up with Gaylord Focker (Ben Stiller) engaged to Pam (Teri Polo). Pam's father, ex-CIA operative Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro), wants to size up in his future son-in-law's parents, and so, the four of them, together with Jack's infant grandson, hit the road in a high-tech trailer to meet Gaylord's mom and dad.

When the Byrneses arrive, they are met by a bare-chested, overly gregarious Bernie Focker (Dustin Hoffman), from whose sloppy welcoming kisses Jack recoils, while sex therapist wife Roz (Barbra Streisand) is in the midst of a class for seniors. Though the Fockers pretend she's merely teaching yoga, the Byrneses, especially Jack, are appalled. (Eventually, Roz will attempt to loosen the uptight Jack by giving him a sensual massage.)

Jack is turned off by the Fockers' bohemian lifestyle, and insists that the family sleep in the trailer rather than under the Fockers' roof, but a riotous chase between the Byrneses' cat and the Fockers' dog ends with the cat flushing the dog down the toilet, and wreaking such havoc in the trailer that they are forced to sleep in the house after all.

Before long, Pam tells Gaylord she's pregnant, a fact that Roz already intuits, and eventually everyone knows the truth except Jack.

Over dinner one night, it is revealed that the buxom Latino cook, Isabel (Alanna Ubach), once had an affair with Gaylord. Later, when Jack meets her illegitimate son, who bears a striking resemblance to Gaylord, Jack assumes Gaylord's been hiding a secret progeny.

A disastrous dinner involving Gaylord's uncircumcised foreskin, a game of touch football where Jack is decked by Bernie, and a calamitous baby-sitting episode with Gaylord taking care of his fiancee's nephew are among the other comic set pieces, which range from amusing to yuck-inducing.

"Meet the Fockers" is also notable for bringing Streisand back to the screen for the first time in eight years. Sporting the Shirley Temple curls she had in 1976's "A Star Is Born," and now a bit plump, if tanned and happy, she gives an uninhibited performance that recalls her early comedies like "For Pete's Sake" and "The Main Event."

The cast is first-rate across the board, and they seem to be having a jolly time, however dubious the proceedings.

Though the film ultimately espouses good family values, much of the plot is intentionally tasteless and the language and situations mostly on the crude side. The humor -- much of the bedroom and bathroom kind -- often crosses the bad-taste threshold.

This film contains sexual situations and innuendo, coarse language and brief rear nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
